coherence.reasons: Both run the same logical spine (market, unit economics, customers, cash, options, decision), and in both the executive summary maps cleanly onto the slides. Y is tighter: it opens by splitting the founders' case into three claims with verdicts, and every later slide supports one of those verdicts. X is consistent overall but has small internal tensions. Slide 26 says 'Density, not store count, is the lever', while slide 34 says no amount of density fixes the loss per order and slide 14 shows density as the smallest of the four drivers. Slide 8 says Zipcart's profit came 'not from scale' while also noting it was the densest city. X's slide 12 title ('orders pay their own way') is on a before-site-cost basis, which sits awkwardly beside the after-site-cost governing numbers.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation: decline the launch, scale the software, add store-based delivery for grocers, and set reopen gates. Both weigh the same three options and reject the one-store pilot on runway grounds. Y adds two things the key values: the pilot 'would retest what 14 sites and the pop-up already show; scaling it brings back option A' (the stealth risk), and a reopen trigger qualified by promotions at or below 6%, which stops a promotion-bought result passing the gate. Y also states the plan's upside (about +$12M a year) and admits that the core business itself hits the runway floor in about 18 months at flat burn, so burn must fall whatever the board decides. X's advantage is a quantified software path to break-even (early 2029, about $5.4M left), which speaks directly to the investors' objective. But it rests on 60% growth continuing with costs held flat, an optimistic assumption, though X flags it. Net, Y's trade-off handling is slightly sharper.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: median −$6.17, best composite −$1.76, pop-up −$12.57, $2.5M and about 6 months of runway, Zipcart-playbook at median −$1.05, and payback of about 15 months on plan. I recomputed their derived figures and found no numerical errors in either. Y adds more decision-relevant derivations: an explicit 41.5% CAGR; density explains only about a fifth of the plan-to-benchmark gap; about 6,400 orders a day needed at the best composite margin; the pop-up still loses $9.71 at 900 orders a day; any two misses make the plan negative; and the 14 benchmark sites already run Parcelbird software, so the claimed edge is already in the numbers. X adds a useful break-even basket ($63), a 20% sensitivity table and a rider-pay sensitivity. X's weaker points are a software projection built on unsupported flat-cost and 60%-growth assumptions (labelled as an estimate) and the inference that Zipcart's profit came 'not from scale'. Y's weaker point is the title 'nothing in the evidence supports +$2', which slightly overclaims because a fee at best density would be positive. Neither computes the fee-at-best-density case. Y edges it on precision and sharper use of the critical evidence.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis and keep the part the evidence supports (growth above 40%). Y handles it more explicitly and rigorously. Its slide 3 separates the three founder claims and gives each a verdict: growth holds; 'we run stores better than anyone' is not supported, because the benchmark sites already use Parcelbird software and the company's own pop-up underperformed them; 'density fixes it' is not supported, because density explains only $1.75 of the $8.19 gap and break-even density would be about 6,400 orders a day. That is a direct, evidence-based dismantling of the density hypothesis. X also confirms growth, shows the plan needs all four drivers above the best site, and flags 'nobody owns the Midwest' as untested, but it never confronts the 'we run them better' claim head-on and is less pointed on density. Both engage with the Zipcart counter-evidence to a similar degree.

overall.reasons: The two documents reach the same defensible recommendation with correct core calculations, so the difference is in sharpness. Y would serve the board better: it confronts the founders' claims directly, supplies the most telling derived facts (density is a fifth of the gap, the software edge is already in the benchmarks, the pilot leads back to option A), is candid about the core business's own burn problem, and ends with crisp decisions and gaming-resistant triggers. X is thorough and adds a useful software break-even projection and sensitivities, but that projection rests on optimistic assumptions and the document carries a few minor internal inconsistencies. Its extra length adds little decision-relevant reasoning beyond Y.
